import ProblemCard from '../../components/ProblemCard.astro';

<section id="ch5-sec2" class="ed-sec-block">

### 5.2 The Biot-Savart Law

<div class="ed-theory-box">

**Steady Currents (§5.2.1).** Magnetostatics is the study of magnetic fields generated by *steady currents*—continuous flows of charge in which neither the charge density nor the current density changes with time:

$$
\frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} = 0, \qquad \frac{\partial \vec{J}}{\partial t} = \vec{0}.
$$

In this regime, the continuity equation $\nabla \cdot \vec{J} = -\partial \rho / \partial t$ reduces to the solenoidality condition

$$
\nabla \cdot \vec{J} = 0.
$$

For a filamentary wire carrying a steady current $I$, this requires $I$ to have the same magnitude everywhere along the circuit. Unlike electrostatics—which can be built from stationary point charges via superposition—a moving point charge does not constitute a steady current ($\partial \rho / \partial t \neq 0$ and $\partial \vec{J} / \partial t \neq 0$), so magnetostatics must be formulated directly in terms of extended steady current distributions.

**The Biot-Savart Law (§5.2.2).** The magnetic field at field point $\vec{r}$ due to a steady line current $I$ along a closed path is given by the Biot-Savart law:

$$
\vec{B}(\vec{r}) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi} \int \frac{d\vec{l}' \times (\vec{r} - \vec{r}')}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}'|^3},
$$

where $d\vec{l}'$ is an infinitesimal displacement along the wire in the direction of the current at source point $\vec{r}'$, and $\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\text{ N/A}^2$ is the permeability of free space. The SI unit of $\vec{B}$ is the tesla ($1\text{ T} = 1\text{ N/(A}\cdot\text{m)} = 10^4\text{ gauss}$). For steady surface currents $\vec{K}(\vec{r}')$ and volume currents $\vec{J}(\vec{r}')$, the Biot-Savart law generalizes to

$$
\vec{B}(\vec{r}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \int_S \frac{\vec{K}(\vec{r}') \times (\vec{r} - \vec{r}')}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}'|^3}\,da', \qquad \vec{B}(\vec{r}) = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} \int_V \frac{\vec{J}(\vec{r}') \times (\vec{r} - \vec{r}')}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}'|^3}\,d\tau'.
$$

Magnetic fields obey the superposition principle. However, substituting $I\,d\vec{l}' \to q\vec{v}$ to write $\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0 q}{4\pi}\frac{\vec{v}\times(\vec{r}-\vec{r}')}{|\vec{r}-\vec{r}'|^3}$ for a moving point charge is invalid in general (it holds only as a quasi-static approximation for $v \ll c$), because a single moving charge is not a steady current.

**Canonical Results (Straight Wires and Circular Loops).**
For a straight wire segment at perpendicular distance $s$ from the field point, spanning angles $\theta_1$ to $\theta_2$ measured from the perpendicular bisector ray, the field magnitude is

$$
B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi s}(\sin\theta_2 - \sin\theta_1).
$$

For an infinite straight wire ($\theta_1 = -\pi/2$, $\theta_2 = \pi/2$), this gives $\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi s}\hat{\phi}$ circling the wire by the right-hand rule. Consequently, two long parallel wires separated by distance $d$ carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ exert a force per unit length $f = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$ (attractive if parallel, repulsive if antiparallel). On the symmetry axis of a circular loop of radius $R$ carrying current $I$, at height $z$ above the center,

$$
\vec{B}(z) = \frac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2(R^2 + z^2)^{3/2}}\hat{z}, \qquad B(0) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}.
$$

</div>

<ProblemCard num="5.6" title="Current Densities of a Rotating Disk and a Spinning Sphere" tag="Griffiths 5.6 · Steady Currents">

<div slot="problem">

(a) A phonograph record carries a uniform density of "static electricity" $\sigma$. If it rotates at angular velocity $\omega$, what is the surface current density $\vec{K}$ at a distance $r$ from the center?

(b) A uniformly charged solid sphere, of radius $R$ and total charge $Q$, is centered at the origin and spinning at a constant angular velocity $\omega$ about the $z$ axis. Find the volume current density $\vec{J}$ at any point $(r, \theta, \phi)$ within the sphere.

</div>

<div slot="answer">

(a) $\vec{K}(r) = \sigma \omega r\,\hat{\phi}$ (magnitude $K = \sigma \omega r$, directed azimuthally along the motion).

(b) $\vec{J}(r, \theta, \phi) = \rho \omega r \sin\theta\,\hat{\phi} = \dfrac{3Q\omega}{4\pi R^3} r \sin\theta\,\hat{\phi}$.

</div>

<div slot="solution">

**(a)** In cylindrical coordinates $(r, \phi, z)$ with the disk in the $xy$ plane rotating about the $z$ axis at angular velocity $\vec{\omega} = \omega\hat{z}$, a point on the record at radial distance $r$ from the center moves with tangential velocity

$$
\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r} = \omega r\,\hat{\phi}.
$$

Since the surface carries a uniform surface charge density $\sigma$, the surface current density is $\vec{K} = \sigma \vec{v}$, giving

$$
\vec{K}(r) = \sigma \omega r\,\hat{\phi}.
$$

**(b)** The solid sphere of radius $R$ and total charge $Q$ has a uniform volume charge density

$$
\rho = \frac{Q}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3} = \frac{3Q}{4\pi R^3}.
$$

For rigid-body rotation about the $z$ axis with $\vec{\omega} = \omega\hat{z}$, a point inside the sphere at spherical coordinates $(r, \theta, \phi)$ lies at perpendicular distance $s = r\sin\theta$ from the $z$ axis and therefore has velocity

$$
\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r} = \omega r \sin\theta\,\hat{\phi}.
$$

Using $\vec{J} = \rho\vec{v}$, the volume current density at any point inside the sphere ($r < R$) is

$$
\vec{J}(r, \theta, \phi) = \rho\omega r\sin\theta\,\hat{\phi} = \frac{3Q\omega}{4\pi R^3} r\sin\theta\,\hat{\phi}.
$$

Note that although both distributions are rotating, $\partial\rho/\partial t = 0$ and $\partial\vec{J}/\partial t = \vec{0}$ everywhere because the charge distributions are azimuthally symmetric; hence both produce steady currents.

</div>

</ProblemCard>

<ProblemCard num="5.7" title="Volume Integral of Current Density and Dipole Moment" tag="Griffiths 5.7 · Continuity Equation">

<div slot="problem">

For a configuration of charges and currents confined within a volume $V$, show that

$$
\int_V \vec{J}\,d\tau = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt},
$$

where $\vec{p}$ is the total electric dipole moment. [Hint: evaluate $\int_V \nabla \cdot (x\vec{J})\,d\tau$.]

</div>

<div slot="answer">

Using $\dfrac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} = -\nabla\cdot\vec{J}$ together with the product rule $\nabla\cdot(x\vec{J}) = x(\nabla\cdot\vec{J}) + J_x$ and the divergence theorem (with $\vec{J}=\vec{0}$ on the boundary $\partial V$), one obtains $\displaystyle \int_V \vec{J}\,d\tau = -\int_V (\nabla\cdot\vec{J})\vec{r}\,d\tau = \frac{d}{dt}\int_V \rho\vec{r}\,d\tau = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$.

</div>

<div slot="solution">

The total electric dipole moment of the charge distribution inside the fixed volume $V$ is $\vec{p} = \int_V \rho(\vec{r}, t)\vec{r}\,d\tau$. Differentiating with respect to time and applying the continuity equation $\partial\rho/\partial t = -\nabla\cdot\vec{J}$ gives

$$
\frac{d\vec{p}}{dt} = \int_V \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t}\vec{r}\,d\tau = -\int_V (\nabla\cdot\vec{J})\vec{r}\,d\tau.
$$

To evaluate the $x$ component, apply the divergence product rule to the vector field $x\vec{J}$:

$$
\nabla \cdot (x\vec{J}) = x(\nabla \cdot \vec{J}) + \vec{J} \cdot (\nabla x).
$$

Since $\nabla x = \hat{x}$, we have $\vec{J}\cdot(\nabla x) = J_x$, so

$$
\nabla \cdot (x\vec{J}) = x(\nabla \cdot \vec{J}) + J_x.
$$

Integrating over $V$ and invoking the divergence theorem on the left-hand side, where $S = \partial V$ is the boundary surface enclosing $V$:

$$
\oint_S x\vec{J}\cdot d\vec{a} = \int_V x(\nabla\cdot\vec{J})\,d\tau + \int_V J_x\,d\tau.
$$

Because all charges and currents are confined strictly within $V$, $\vec{J} = \vec{0}$ on the bounding surface $S$, so the surface integral vanishes identically. Thus,

$$
\int_V J_x\,d\tau = -\int_V x(\nabla\cdot\vec{J})\,d\tau = \frac{dp_x}{dt}.
$$

Repeating the exact same steps with $y\vec{J}$ and $z\vec{J}$ yields $\int_V J_y\,d\tau = dp_y/dt$ and $\int_V J_z\,d\tau = dp_z/dt$. Combining all three components gives

$$
\int_V \vec{J}\,d\tau = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}.
$$

*(Quick check for discrete point charges: if $\vec{J}(\vec{r}) = \sum_i q_i \vec{v}_i \delta^3(\vec{r} - \vec{r}_i)$, then $\int_V \vec{J}\,d\tau = \sum_i q_i \vec{v}_i = \frac{d}{dt}\sum_i q_i \vec{r}_i = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$.)*

</div>

</ProblemCard>

<ProblemCard num="5.8" title="Magnetic Field at the Center of Regular Polygonal Loops" tag="Griffiths 5.8 · Biot-Savart Law">

<div slot="problem">

(a) Find the magnetic field at the center of a square loop, which carries a steady current $I$. Let $R$ be the distance from center to side.

(b) Find the field at the center of a regular $n$-sided polygon, carrying a steady current $I$. Again, let $R$ be the distance from the center to any side.

(c) Check that your formula reduces to the field at the center of a circular loop in the limit $n \to \infty$.

</div>

<div slot="answer">

(a) $B = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}\,\mu_0 I}{\pi R}$ (perpendicular to the plane of the loop, by the right-hand rule).

(b) $B = \dfrac{n\mu_0 I}{2\pi R}\sin\!\left(\dfrac{\pi}{n}\right)$.

(c) As $n \to \infty$, $\sin(\pi/n) \approx \pi/n$, so $B \to \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$, matching the field at the center of a circular loop of radius $R$.

</div>

<div slot="solution">

**(a)** A straight wire segment at perpendicular distance $s$ from the field point produces a magnetic field of magnitude

$$
B_{\text{seg}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi s}(\sin\theta_2 - \sin\theta_1),
$$

where $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are the angles from the perpendicular line to the two ends of the segment. For one side of the square, the perpendicular distance from the center to the side is $s = R$, and the side subtends a total angle of $90^\circ$ at the center, so $\theta_1 = -45^\circ = -\pi/4$ and $\theta_2 = +45^\circ = +\pi/4$. Hence each side contributes

$$
B_{\text{side}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\left[\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right) - \sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right] = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = \frac{\sqrt{2}\,\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}.
$$

By the right-hand rule, all four sides produce fields in the same direction (normal to the plane of the loop). Summing over the $4$ sides yields

$$
B = 4 B_{\text{side}} = \frac{\sqrt{2}\,\mu_0 I}{\pi R}.
$$

**(b)** For a regular $n$-sided polygon of apothem $R$ (center-to-side distance), each side subtends a central angle of $2\pi/n$, so $\theta_1 = -\pi/n$ and $\theta_2 = +\pi/n$ with $s = R$. The contribution of a single side is

$$
B_{\text{side}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\left[\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right) - \sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{n}\right)\right] = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right).
$$

Because all $n$ sides add constructively in the same direction perpendicular to the polygon, the total field at the center is

$$
B = n B_{\text{side}} = \frac{n\mu_0 I}{2\pi R}\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right).
$$

*(Checking $n = 4$ recovers $\frac{4\mu_0 I}{2\pi R}\sin(\pi/4) = \frac{\sqrt{2}\,\mu_0 I}{\pi R}$.)*

**(c)** In the limit $n \to \infty$, the angle $\pi/n$ becomes small, so $\sin(\pi/n) = \frac{\pi}{n} - \frac{1}{6}\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right)^3 + \cdots$. Substituting the leading term gives

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty} B = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{n\mu_0 I}{2\pi R}\left(\frac{\pi}{n}\right) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R},
$$

which is precisely the magnetic field at the center of a circular loop of radius $R$ (Eq. 5.41 evaluated at $z = 0$).

</div>

</ProblemCard>

<ProblemCard num="5.9" title="Magnetic Field of Piecewise Circular and Straight Loops" tag="Griffiths 5.9 · Superposition & Biot-Savart">

<div slot="problem">

Find the magnetic field at point $P$ for each of the steady current configurations shown:

(a) A closed loop formed by two concentric quarter-circular arcs of inner radius $a$ and outer radius $b$ centered at $P$, connected by two radial straight segments along lines passing through $P$ (with current flowing counterclockwise along the inner arc and clockwise along the outer arc).

(b) A hairpin-shaped wire formed by two parallel semi-infinite straight segments separated by distance $2R$, joined smoothly by a semicircular arc of radius $R$ centered at $P$ (with current flowing toward the semicircle along the upper line, clockwise around the semicircle, and away from it along the lower line).

</div>

<div slot="answer">

(a) $\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{8}\left(\dfrac{1}{a} - \dfrac{1}{b}\right)$ out of the page.

(b) $\vec{B} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{4R}\left(1 + \dfrac{2}{\pi}\right)$ into the page.

</div>

<div slot="solution">

**(a)** By the Biot-Savart law, the contribution of any differential element $d\vec{l}'$ to $\vec{B}(P)$ is proportional to $d\vec{l}' \times (\vec{r}_P - \vec{r}')$. Along the two radial straight segments, $d\vec{l}'$ is collinear with the displacement vector $\vec{r}_P - \vec{r}'$ pointing toward or away from $P$, so $d\vec{l}' \times (\vec{r}_P - \vec{r}') = \vec{0}$ and neither straight segment produces any field at $P$.

For a circular arc of radius $r$ subtending an angle $\Delta\phi$ at its center, every element satisfies $|d\vec{l}' \times (\vec{r}_P - \vec{r}')| = r\,dl'$ with $|\vec{r}_P - \vec{r}'| = r$, so

$$
B_{\text{arc}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi} \int_0^{\Delta\phi} \frac{r\,d\phi}{r^2} = \frac{\mu_0 I\,\Delta\phi}{4\pi r}.
$$

For a quarter-circle ($\Delta\phi = \pi/2$), this gives $B_{\text{quarter}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{8r}$. By the right-hand rule, the inner arc of radius $a$ (counterclockwise) produces a field $\frac{\mu_0 I}{8a}$ out of the page, while the outer arc of radius $b$ (clockwise) produces a field $\frac{\mu_0 I}{8b}$ into the page. Since $a < b$, the net magnetic field at $P$ is

$$
B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{8a} - \frac{\mu_0 I}{8b} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{8}\left(\frac{1}{a} - \frac{1}{b}\right) \quad \text{(out of the page)}.
$$

**(b)** Place $P$ at the origin $(0, 0)$ with the two semi-infinite straight wires along $y = +R$ and $y = -R$ for $x \le 0$, joined by the semicircle of radius $R$ in the half-plane $x \ge 0$.

1. **Two semi-infinite straight segments:** Both segments lie at perpendicular distance $s = R$ from $P$. For the upper wire ($x$ from $-\infty$ to $0$ at $y = +R$, current in the $+\hat{x}$ direction), $\theta_1 = -\pi/2$ and $\theta_2 = 0$, so

$$
B_{\text{upper}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\left[\sin(0) - \sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right] = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R},
$$

pointing into the page by the right-hand rule. For the lower wire ($x$ from $0$ to $-\infty$ at $y = -R$, current in the $-\hat{x}$ direction), $P$ lies above the wire while the current flows left, so by the right-hand rule its field at $P$ *also* points into the page with the same magnitude $\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}$. Together, the two semi-infinite wires produce the same field as a single infinite wire at distance $R$:

$$
B_{\text{lines}} = 2\left(\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi R}\right) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R} \quad \text{(into the page)}.
$$

2. **Semicircular arc:** Using $B_{\text{arc}} = \frac{\mu_0 I\,\Delta\phi}{4\pi R}$ with $\Delta\phi = \pi$, the clockwise semicircle contributes

$$
B_{\text{semi}} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4R} \quad \text{(into the page)}.
$$

Adding both contributions (which point in the same direction, into the page) gives

$$
B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4R} + \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi R} = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4R}\left(1 + \frac{2}{\pi}\right) \quad \text{(into the page)}.
$$

</div>

</ProblemCard>

<ProblemCard num="5.10" title="Magnetic Force on Square and Triangular Loops Near a Wire" tag="Griffiths 5.10 · Lorentz Force on Currents">

<div slot="problem">

(a) Find the force on a square loop of side $a$ placed with its nearest edge at distance $s$ from an infinite straight wire. Both the loop and the wire carry a steady current $I$ (with current flowing to the right in the wire and clockwise around the loop).

(b) Find the force on an equilateral triangular loop of side $a$ whose base is parallel to the infinite straight wire at distance $s$, and whose apex points away from the wire at distance $s + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a$ (again with current $I$ to the right in the wire and clockwise around the loop).

</div>

<div slot="answer">

(a) $\vec{F} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I^2 a^2}{2\pi s(s + a)}\,\hat{y}$ (upward, away from the wire).

(b) $\vec{F} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi}\left[\dfrac{a}{s} - \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\ln\!\left(1 + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}\,a}{2s}\right)\right]\hat{y}$ (upward, away from the wire).

</div>

<div slot="solution">

Let the infinite straight wire lie along the $x$ axis carrying current $I$ in the $+\hat{x}$ direction, and place the loops in the $xy$ plane ($y > 0$). By the Biot-Savart law (Eq. 5.39), the magnetic field of the infinite wire in the upper half-plane $y > 0$ is

$$
\vec{B}(y) = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi y}\,\hat{z} \quad \text{(out of the page)}.
$$

The magnetic force on a current element $I\,d\vec{l}$ is $d\vec{F} = I(d\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$.

**(a) Square loop:** The bottom edge lies at $y = s$ with current flowing left ($-\hat{x}$), and the top edge lies at $y = s + a$ with current flowing right ($+\hat{x}$).

- On the two vertical sides ($x = \text{const}$), the field $\vec{B}(y)$ depends only on $y$, and the currents flow in opposite directions ($+\hat{y}$ on the left side, $-\hat{y}$ on the right side). Hence the horizontal forces on the two vertical sides are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, canceling identically.
- On the bottom edge ($y = s$, $d\vec{l} = -dx\,\hat{x}$ integrated over length $a$):

$$
\vec{F}_{\text{bot}} = I a (-\hat{x}) \times \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi s}\hat{z} = \frac{\mu_0 I^2 a}{2\pi s}\,\hat{y}.
$$

- On the top edge ($y = s + a$, $d\vec{l} = dx\,\hat{x}$ integrated over length $a$):

$$
\vec{F}_{\text{top}} = I a (+\hat{x}) \times \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi(s+a)}\hat{z} = -\frac{\mu_0 I^2 a}{2\pi(s+a)}\,\hat{y}.
$$

Summing all sides gives the net force on the square loop:

$$
\vec{F} = \left[\frac{\mu_0 I^2 a}{2\pi s} - \frac{\mu_0 I^2 a}{2\pi(s + a)}\right]\hat{y} = \frac{\mu_0 I^2 a^2}{2\pi s(s + a)}\,\hat{y} \quad \text{(away from the wire)}.
$$

**(b) Equilateral triangular loop:** The horizontal base of length $a$ at $y = s$ carries current in the $-\hat{x}$ direction, so its force is identical to the bottom edge in part (a):

$$
\vec{F}_{\text{bot}} = \frac{\mu_0 I^2 a}{2\pi s}\,\hat{y}.
$$

For an arbitrary segment in the $xy$ plane with $d\vec{l} = dx\,\hat{x} + dy\,\hat{y}$, the differential force is

$$
d\vec{F} = I(dx\,\hat{x} + dy\,\hat{y}) \times \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi y}\hat{z} = \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi y}\left(-dx\,\hat{y} + dy\,\hat{x}\right).
$$

Along the left slanted side, $y$ increases from $s$ to $s + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a$ while $x$ increases by $a/2$; along the right slanted side, $y$ decreases back from $s + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}a$ to $s$ while $x$ increases by $a/2$. Because $dy$ has opposite signs on the two slanted sides while $y$ ranges over the same values, the $x$ components cancel by symmetry: $F_{x,\text{left}} + F_{x,\text{right}} = 0$.

For the left slanted side, shift the origin of $x$ to the intersection of the extended side with the $x$ axis, so that the line obeys $y = \sqrt{3}\,x$ and $x$ runs from $s/\sqrt{3}$ to $s/\sqrt{3} + a/2$. The vertical force on the left side is

$$
F_{y,\text{left}} = -\frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi} \int_{s/\sqrt{3}}^{s/\sqrt{3} + a/2} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{3}\,x} = -\frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\sqrt{3}\,\pi}\ln\!\left(\frac{s/\sqrt{3} + a/2}{s/\sqrt{3}}\right) = -\frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\sqrt{3}\,\pi}\ln\!\left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}\,a}{2s}\right).
$$

Along the right slanted side, $x$ also increases by $a/2$ as $y$ varies symmetrically over the same heights, so $F_{y,\text{right}} = F_{y,\text{left}}$. Adding the upward force on the base and the downward forces on the two slanted sides gives the net force on the triangle:

$$
\vec{F} = \left[\frac{\mu_0 I^2 a}{2\pi s} - 2 \cdot \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\sqrt{3}\,\pi}\ln\!\left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}\,a}{2s}\right)\right]\hat{y} = \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi}\left[\frac{a}{s} - \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\ln\!\left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}\,a}{2s}\right)\right]\hat{y}.
$$

Since $\ln(1 + u) < u$ for all $u > 0$, we have $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\ln\!\left(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}a}{2s}\right) < \frac{a}{s}$, so the net force is strictly positive (upward, away from the wire). *(In the dipole limit $a \ll s$, expanding $\ln(1+u) \approx u - u^2/2$ gives $F \approx \frac{\mu_0 I^2}{2\pi s^2}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^2\right) = m|\partial B/\partial y|$, where $m = IA$ is the magnetic dipole moment of the triangle.)*

</div>

</ProblemCard>

</section>
